analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers opt into a simple two-rate tax, repeals the individual AMT, and makes capital-gains tax cuts permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 91 Republican sponsors but never received a hearing or vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the alternative minimum tax on individuals, which by 2007 was reaching many middle-class families. It also would have let any individual choose, once, to switch to a simplified tax: 10% on the first $50,000 of income ($100,000 for couples) and 25% above that, with a large standard deduction but no itemized deductions or credits. And it would have permanently extended the reduced 15% tax rates on capital gains and dividends.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners would have gained the most: the top rate would drop from 35% to 25% for anyone who elects the new system, and investors would get permanently lower tax rates on capital gains and dividends. Families caught by the AMT and people who value simple filing would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the individual alternative minimum tax for tax years after 2006, ending a tax originally aimed at the wealthy that increasingly hit middle-class families.
Lets individuals elect a simplified tax with just two rates — 10% up to $50,000 ($100,000 for couples) and 25% above — plus a $12,500/$25,000 standard deduction and personal exemptions.
Makes permanent the 15% maximum rates on capital gains and dividends that were scheduled to expire.
The election window runs through 2016, and the dollar amounts adjust for inflation after 2007.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury: the bill has no revenue offsets, so cutting rates, repealing the AMT, and locking in lower capital gains taxes would have added to deficits or forced matching spending cuts. Taxpayers who elect the new system give up itemized deductions (mortgage interest, state and local taxes, charitable giving) and credits, which could raise taxes for some, especially homeowners in high-tax states.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury, and some itemizing taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no way to pay for the lost revenue, so it would have increased deficits or required offsetting cuts to other programs.

Electing the simplified system means permanently giving up itemized deductions and credits; a taxpayer who opts in can only reverse the choice once, so families whose deductions are worth more could be locked into paying more.

The largest benefits flow to the highest earners and asset owners: a 25% ceiling replacing the 35% top rate, and a permanent 15% capital gains and dividends rate that mainly benefits households that live on investment income.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: AMT repeal and simpler filing are real, broadly shared benefits. But the design is skewed: the top rate falls from 35% to 25% and the investment-income cuts are made permanent, all without any revenue offset. The cost — larger deficits or future spending cuts — lands on everyone, while the biggest gains go to high-income households.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Ryan introduced the bill on October 10, 2007, joined by 33 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, the committee that handles tax legislation.
That was the only action ever taken; no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote followed.
Ninety Republicans had signed on as cosponsors by the end of the Congress.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the revenue the bill would have forgiven, and no offsetting spending cuts or added deficits followed. High earners and investors who would have benefited from the rate cuts gained nothing; families paying the AMT had to wait for later, separately funded relief.

for.name: Rep. Paul Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Taxpayer Choice Act and gathered 33 original cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Charles Rangel)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor — 91 members in all — was a Republican; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic majority that controlled Ways and Means never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would cap the top individual rate at 25% (down from 35%) and make the 15% capital gains and dividends rates permanent, with no revenue offset. Ordinary taxpayers would bear the cost through deficits or future spending cuts.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: An optional two-rate system with a flat standard deduction and no itemized deductions would make filing simple enough for many people to do without paid preparers or software. Their loss would come from the public gaining simplicity.
